content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus (esp. A, C, D) identifies 'rich' primarily as a symbol of spiritual danger: self-sufficiency and misplaced trust in worldly possessions rather than God, often masking spiritual poverty while materially full (Rev 3:17 as the classic ironic text). A well-attested inverted sense — true riches as being 'rich toward God,' rich in faith and grace regardless of material state (Luke 12:21; Rev 2:9; James 2:5; 2 Cor 8:9) — is listed as a common alternative, and Response B even makes the spiritual-wealth sense primary. Other strands (OT blessing, oppressor class, neutral stewardship) are acknowledged as secondary.","book_summary":"The book defines 'rich' as the self-sufficient who claim to 'have need of nothing' — full of self and therefore unable to receive — exemplified by Laodicea's boast, with Smyrna as its opposite. It pairs this with the inverted positive sense: true wealth is being 'rich toward God,' faith tried in the fire, and the garment of righteousness.","consensus_core_identification":"Rich = self-sufficient reliance on worldly abundance instead of God, a deceptive fullness that masks spiritual poverty; with the recognized inversion that true riches are spiritual — being rich toward God in faith and grace.","book_core_identification":"Rich = the self-sufficient who are full of self and unable to receive (Laodicea), contrasted with true riches: being rich toward God, faith refined by fire, righteousness (Smyrna).","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"Minimal. The book compresses the symbol to its ironic/spiritual axis (self-fullness vs. richness toward God) and does not treat the material-wealth-as-hindrance texts (camel and needle, rich fool's possessions) or the OT blessing strand explicitly, but its Laodicea/Smyrna pairing is exactly the consensus's central ironic reading plus its most-cited alternative. Any shift of emphasis from literal wealth to the interior state of self-sufficiency is a difference of framing, not of referent — the consensus itself already frames the symbol as self-sufficiency and deceptive security.","material_contradiction":"None. Nothing in the book entry requires rejecting the consensus identification; it affirms both the dominant negative sense (self-sufficient boast masking spiritual poverty) and the recognized positive inversion (rich toward God).","rationale":"Reduced to minimum cores, both readings identify 'rich' as symbolic self-sufficiency that conceals real spiritual poverty (Rev 3:17), balanced by the inverted true-riches sense (Rev 2:9; Luke 12:21). Every element in the book entry — Laodicea's boast, Smyrna's opposite, richness toward God, the fire-tried gold and white raiment — appears in the consensus responses' primary meanings or their most prominent alternatives. The book adds a devotional gloss ('full of self, and so unable to receive') but this is an elaboration of the same identification, not a change in extension or boundary. This is MATCH, not REFINED, because no cases are added, excluded, or reclassified.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue REFINED on the ground that the book narrows 'rich' to an interior spiritual condition (self-fullness) and omits the material-wealth-as-obstacle cases (rich young ruler, mammon, rich fool's barns) that dominate the consensus's proof texts, thereby quietly excluding literal wealth from the symbol's extension. But the entry does not deny those cases; it simply distills the symbol via its clearest ironic texts, and the consensus itself already centers self-sufficiency as the meaning behind the wealth texts.","confidence":"high"}
